The jewellery trade bought less gold last quarter than in any quarter since the pandemic — and paid more for it.

World Gold Council data puts second-quarter jewellery demand at 278 tonnes, down 17% year on year. The value of that demand rose 14% to $40 billion. One number explains both lines: the quarter averaged $4,506.29 an ounce. At that level the same window holds fewer grams and the same customer goes home with a lighter piece.

Everything else held. Total demand was flat at 1,269 tonnes, bar and coin steady at 307, central banks back to 289 tonnes, ETFs down 45. Investment stayed; jewellery left. Jewellery is the only line in the accounts paid out of a household budget rather than a balance sheet.

Worth noting: gold closed Friday at $4,054.68, about 10% below the quarter's mean. The tonnage that vanished was priced off a level the trade is no longer paying — and the Indian festive build starts in the third quarter.

De Beers spent the first half of 2026 losing money more slowly, and that is the good news.

Anglo American's interim accounts put the diamond unit's revenue at $1.58 billion, 19% lower, with an underlying loss of $188 million — 23% narrower than a year ago. Sales volumes fell 20%. The consolidated realised price fell 32% to $105 a carat, pulled down by a mix weighted to cheaper goods and an index 16% below last year.

The useful numbers are not the losses. They are 68 and 69 — the rough price index in the first and second quarters. Two flat quarters is the first set of figures that supports what De Beers has been arguing since its July sight: that prices have found their level. A cutter cannot fund inventory that reprices underneath him.

It was bought with cuts, not demand. Unit costs fell 26% to $64 a carat, capex fell 33% to $115 million, Venetia is paused for two years and roughly 25 buyers came off the sightholder roster. Anglo says the sale is in its final and most challenging phase, and still will not name a buyer.

Jewelers of America went back to Washington this week, and the ask has narrowed to a single sentence: take diamonds, gemstones and pearls out of the tariff schedule.

The current round applies 10% to 12.5% duties to imports from roughly sixty countries under a forced-labour investigation, effective late July. Seven producing states are exempt — Botswana, Namibia, Kenya, Madagascar, Mozambique, Tanzania and Zambia — and diamonds polished in the European Union keep their exemption. India, which cuts most of the world's polished goods, carries 10%. That single line is the one that reaches most American counters.

The exclusion argument is stronger than it sounds. Rough diamonds and coloured stones are not mined in the United States in commercial quantity, so a duty on them protects no domestic industry. It is collected at the border and paid at the counter.

A second investigation covering India, China, Thailand, the EU and Switzerland is still open, and could catch Swiss watches and Thai colour at the same time. Retailers should not plan on getting the exclusion. Plan the autumn buy at 10% on Indian polished.
